stimulus.text: The engraving, 'The Bloody Massacre perpetrated in King-Street Boston on March 5th 1770,' was engraved, printed, and sold by Paul Revere. It shows a neat line of British soldiers firing a single volley into a crowd of Bostonians, with five men fallen in the foreground. Below the image, the names of the dead are listed: Samuel Gray, Samuel Maverick, James Caldwell, Crispus Attucks, and Patrick Carr — 'Killed. Six wounded.'

books.section: A. Colonial Resistance to British Policies in the Aftermath of the French and Indian War
The Sugar Act, the Currency Act, and the Stamp Act

stem: The trial that followed the Boston Massacre most directly demonstrated which of the following?

options.text: That colonial juries always convicted British soldiers
options.misconception: The jury acquitted six of the eight soldiers — the opposite of always convicting, and the verdict came from a colonial court.

options.text: That Samuel Adams controlled the Massachusetts courts
options.misconception: Adams spread the propaganda, but he did not control the court — John Adams, his cousin, defended the soldiers, and the jury decided on the evidence.

options.text: That Patriots gave the accused a fair trial
That Parliament immediately withdrew all troops from Boston
options.misconception: The troops were not withdrawn after the trial — they remained in Boston, and tensions continued until the Tea Party four years later.

rationales.C: Background: John Adams — a leading Patriot — defended the soldiers in court, and six of the eight were acquitted. The Patriots who denounced the Massacre still gave the accused a fair trial, with a defense lawyer and a jury.
rationales.A: The jury acquitted six of eight. A court that always convicted would not have done that.
rationales.B: Samuel Adams had no control over the court. His cousin John defended the soldiers, and the jury weighed the evidence.
rationales.D: The troops had already left the town for Castle William in Boston Harbor in March 1770, before the trial — so there was no withdrawal to follow it, and Boston's tensions carried on to 1773.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who defended the accused. John Adams, a leading Patriot — the same side that called the shooting a massacre.
2. Ask what the verdict was. Six of the eight soldiers were acquitted; two received only a brand on the thumb.
3. Ask what that shows. The Patriots' commitment to a fair trial held even for the men they denounced — a principle applied to their enemies, not just their friends.
Remember: a principle is proved by its hardest case — a fair trial for the accused is the test, not the exception.
